Yusoff’s theory of inhumanism offers unique insight into dispossession through geology, and how geopower is deployed as a tool of empire building.

Low’s report goes into detail on the history of those considered fully human within the western settler mindset. In Chapter IV, A Historical Summary of the Discoveries and Explorations in Arctic America, Low summarizes the Arctic expeditions of white men before him, beginning with Frobisher in 1576. In his writing,
European scientists are named individuals, and Inuit are unnamed, ascribed as property to Europeans
. This parallels the writing of Sir Charles Lyell, president of

Kathryn Yusoff notes Lyell’s writing moves between “‘Geology and Cretaceous strata’ and ‘Montgomery. Curfew. Sunday School for Negros’ in one chapter … and ‘Distinct Table for Coloured and White Passengers’ and ‘Fossil Shells’ in another” (Yusoff, 2018: 81). While white European explorers are named individuals in Low’s account, the chapters on Inuit (called by the slur Eskimo in the report) are structured similarly to chapters on geological inventories themselves. Indeed, Low spends a nearly equivalent portion of his report detailing Inuit lives (52 pages) as he does geological observations (65 pages), cataloguing belief systems and measuring and photographing Inuit. In the appendix of Low’s account, he includes charts detailing the size of Inuit bodies prepared by Dr. Borden, along with extensive photographs documenting clothing, homes, and material culture.

Geological examinations were made on these land journeys, as well as at every ship's halt, and large collections were made of rocks and fossils, northern birds, eggs and nests, skins and skeletons of animals, fishes and marine invertebrates, and plants and insects. Eskimos were studied, and a census was taken. Observations were recorded of the weather, ice conditions and movements, tides and currents, and the habitats and distribution of the whales, seals, walrus, caribou, and muskox of the region. (Zazlow, 1975: 173, emphasis added)
In this way, Inuit were aligned by the survey team with the landscape, drawing an axis of inhumanism through their method of practicing geology.

And much like the efforts of the survey team to exert sovereignty over the territory through planting flags, the team set out to exert sovereignty over Inuit. At the turn of the century, as Canada took an interest in establishing their presence in the Arctic, the Neptune GSC survey trip brought changes to Inuit and non-Inuit residents of the Arctic Archipelago. Major Moodie, a member of the Northwest Mounted Police (NWMP), traveled north with the scientists to establish a permanent police presence. As an occupying police force in a sparsely populated area, the NWMP were granted broad administrative powers – and while they were primarily interested in disrupting the activities of foreign whalers, who were seen as a threat to sovereignty claims (Ross, 1976), Inuit lives came to be reshaped by the decisions of the NWMP (Qikiqtani Inuit Association, 2013). While the Canadian government did not seek a treaty with Inuit, and avoided considering Inuit as wards of the state, policing Inuit came to be the pivotal action that led to government recognition of the fact these people had been colonized when Charles Stewart argued in Parliament in 1925 that the government exercised Canadian law on Inuit through trials, imprisonment, and execution (Duffy, 1988: 7). This policing was put in force when Major Moody set up a meeting with Inuit and set out to describe the role he saw himself playing. The officer arranged a ceremony for several Inuit families, offering gifts along with an explanation of the structure of the Dominion of Canada and the British Empire:

The Major had about eight gallons of tea made and with five pounds of hard tack and other biscuits soon disappeared. A clay pipe and a bit of tobacco was given to each of the twenty-five natives present. Then through the interpreter the Major told the natives that there was a big chief over them all who had many tribes of different colours and how this big chief, who was King Edward VII, had the welfare of all his peoples at heart. King Edward wanted them all to do what was right and good, and had sent the Major as his personal representative or in other words the King could not come himself so 'I was to act for him'! The Major wanted them to do what was right and good and to settle all quarrels but he would punish all offenders. (Borden 1903-04, p. 38)

Like the flag raising on the islands they encountered, the survey team brought police to claim ownership of all Inuit through a brief display – a short spectacle preceding decades of imposition of colonial law, continuing into the present. As such, the Canadian effort to claim
the geologic resources of the Arctic and the bodily resources of Inuit
, who were expected to hunt and guide survey teams, and eventually work in mines and military outposts,
they enable have consequences; they establish unfolding geo-logics, for particular bodies and subject positions, as disposable in the shadow economy of extraction”

his ongoing collection of Inuit skeletons

His collection begins with “a very well preserved skull – no doubt, of a very ancient Eskimo” (Borden, 1903-1904: 102) and he laments that another team member found a skull but did not bring it back to the boat (ibid: 103). While some skulls he found did not end up in his collection as they were allegedly too fresh (ibid: 117) Borden writes about taking the entire body of an Inuk woman, saying “it was a pretty hard, nasty job but it will make a fine skeleton & is now sunk in the sea to be cleaned” (ibid: 106). He went about this removal clandestinely, and writes about the confinement of a dog suspected of taking several of the skeletons he himself removed:

The dog, which had been confined on the island, as the suspected robber of the grave which I had robbed for my skeletons, (noted earlier) was being fed by N.W.M.P. men. For, if he died, he was guilty, but if he survived, innocent. I therefore left word with the N.W.M.P. men to see that he had plenty of food. (Ibid: 131)

The geological relations first established by Martin Frobisher, and reinforced by Low and the GSC, underpinned eventual Inuit land claims negotiations, ensuring that territory and mineral resources were the central negotiation pieces.
